items.summary: Anthropic raised more than US$81 billion (S$105 billion) on Nov 19, topping SpaceX's US$75 billion base deal to become the biggest initial public offering in history. Its shares closed at US$97.17, more than 17% above their offer price. Yet the debut did little to lift sentiment as technology stocks continued facing selling pressure over valuation concerns and heavy AI spending: Nvidia fell 3.3%, Micron Technology declined 2.1%, while the Nasdaq Composite dropped 2.25% and the S&P 500 dipped 2.02%. Analyst Zavier Wong of eToro attributed the broad sell-off to expectations of further US rate hikes, scrutiny over chip exports, a short-selling report on Advanced Micro Devices, Nvidia's loss of its earnings gains amid Jensen Huang's departure, and an interest-rate hike in December that is largely priced in; he noted the S&P 500 had fallen for six consecutive sessions and was down about 8% from October's record high. Gold saw its worst weekly decline since March, tumbling about 7% to hover just above US$3,500 as expectations of further rate hikes and equity-cover selling weighed on it; the metal is down 8.5% in 2026 and is 37% below January's intraday peak of US$5,602. CMC Markets' Alex Ho said the yield on the benchmark 10-year US Treasury note had risen above 5%, while real yields climbed from 2.66% to 2.88% since Nov 9, making interest-free gold less attractive; he argued a lasting recovery needs gold back above US$3,850 to US$3,900 unless real yields and the dollar ease, with tests set for the Fed's Dec 8-9 meeting and US inflation data on Dec 10. The decline also weighed on Singapore-listed gold stocks: CNMC Goldmine Holdings fell 13.61% over the week to close at 82 cents (down about 60% from its March record of $2.12), while ValueMax Group and MoneyMax Financial Services shares fell 8.7% to 74 cents and declined 6.25% to 45 cents respectively on Nov 20. The Straits Times Index dipped below 5,000 points for the first time in six months, falling to a low of 4,980.81 before closing at 4,972.23; local banks declined with DBS down 5.26% over the week to $66.11, OCBC down 7.3% to $26.54, and UOB down 6.17% to $35.42 on Nov 20. Separately, HomesToLife secured an SGX dual listing with a placement of 7.5 million shares at $1.15 each, raising some $8.6 million in gross proceeds; for its FY2025 it reported $19.4 million in operating profit, a 103.7% increase from the previous year, though freight rates rose 22% due to Suez Canal disruptions.
items.title: Anthropic's record IPO contrasted with a broad tech and gold sell-off in Singapore markets

items.summary: Investors are betting that humanoid robots will soon become commonplace, with the Chinese government pledging more than £100bn in robotics investment over two decades while Tesla redirected factories toward its Optimus robot. The central obstacle remains replicating human dexterity: a hand surgeon at University College London describes how 27 bones and dense sensory feedback let us adjust grip within about a tenth of a second, making hands one of the hardest things to reproduce. Robot-hand prices are dropping sharply—Shadow Robot’s full system costs £100,000 while some Chinese models cost less than £2,000—and the number of competitors has grown from four or five companies ten years ago to 110 on a single analyst firm's list, with state media valuing China's domestic dexterous hand industry at more than 50bn yuan (£5.6bn) last year. Experts disagree on timing: Professor Nathan Lepora sees general tool use possible by the end of this decade and Amazon fulfilment workers as soon to be automated, while Shadow Robot’s Rich Walker argues full automation is several hundred years away; even a surgeon who finds autonomous operation very difficult acknowledges that no career is necessarily safe.
items.title: The quest to build a human-level robotic hand is intensifying as prices fall and competitors multiply.

visual.alt: Bar chart. hand 20,000 £; model costs 60,000 £; some hands in China are less 2,000 £.

items.summary: The Intelligence's free Cool Tools newsletter promotes Bigwords.page, a website described as doing one thing: converting any screen into an instant, impossible-to-miss poster for viewing from distance. The tool reportedly keeps the device awake to prevent sleep like a video would, positioning itself against the practical drawbacks of physical posters—preparation time, carrying them, and crumpling in traffic. All claims are promotional assertions by the newsletter's publisher rather than independently verified features.
items.title: Bigwords.page turns smartphone screens into on-demand billboards

items.summary: Baseten released two open-weight decision models—bison-1 and groundhog-1—built on Google's Gemma 4 base; unlike text-generating LLMs, they return calibrated probabilities for yes/no, choice, and score questions with no output tokens. Bison-1 is a 31B dense model that post-trains Gemma 4 31B using soft labels (probability targets instead of one fixed correct answer), which Baseten credits for its lowest index Brier score of 0.14 versus d1.2-ultra's 0.15; groundhog-1 is a cheaper 26B-A4B mixture-of-experts model with about 4B active parameters per token and no official index score yet, which the outlet notes means every number for it is self-reported. Both raise context from 16k to 128k tokens (131,072) and accept images; bison-1 scores 76 on Artificial Analysis Decision Index v2.1—ranked #1 of 19—and ranks first on four of six components including When2Call at 98 (#1), while its weakest component is knowledge-heavy AA-Omniscience-Decision v1.1 at 60 (rank #11). On long context, Baseten reports LongMemEval M(128k) of 84.8 for bison-1 versus 77.4 for groundhog-1; the outlet expects groundhog-1 to match mammoth-1 but flags this as an expectation rather than a measured result. Both models run on Baseten Model APIs and open BF16 weights on Hugging Face, with no inference GPU or quantized builds listed; bison-1 costs $0.10 per 1M input tokens (like the older mammoth-1) while groundhog-1 costs $0.035 (like elephant-1), reflecting their relative sizes and active-parameter counts.
items.title: Baseten releases bison-1 and groundhog-1 decision models on Gemma 4; bison-1 tops Artificial Analysis Decision Index v2.1 at 76, one point above Liquid AI's d1.2-ultra (75)

visual.alt: Bar chart. model scores 76; scores 76; scores 76; scores 71.

items.summary: Bruce Schneier argues that a cluster of recent infrastructure failures—outages at Microsoft, the FAA, several banks, United Airlines, an unnamed classified NSA network, and Apple—are unrelated coincidences rather than evidence of a coordinated or AI-driven cyber-attack. He attributes the fragility to modern shareholder capitalism and private equity prioritizing near-term profits over reliability measures like security, safety, redundancy, and recoverability, which are costs that don't generate revenue; monopolization further removes market competition as an efficiency nudge. Schneier contends these systems operate just at the edge of functionality while pushing failure costs onto society through stranded travelers or inaccessible bank accounts, making them brittle with single points of failure and cascading consequences. He asserts such failures will persist until economic incentives change via regulation with enforcement and meaningful fines plus stringent antitrust action—difficult in the US where monied interests dominate legislation—and warns to expect more outages until then.
items.title: Schneier: recent US tech outages stem from economic incentives, not cyber-attacks

items.summary: Appleyard Lees' sixth annual Inside Green Innovation: Progress Report attributes the divergence to solid-state electrolytes showing strongest growth while lithium-ion technologies appear consolidating after two consecutive years of declines. The report tracks complete public patent data through December 31, 2024, given delays across regions in visibility of applications; Patent volume is generally a lagging indicator of R&D spend.
items.title: Solid-state battery patents hit a record 2,230 in 2024 as lithium-ion filings fell nearly 15%

items.summary: The National Wealth Fund announced an equity investment alongside Matrix Renewables UK Limited to develop two large-scale battery energy storage system (BESS) projects at Eccles and Kilmarnock, Scotland. The combined facilities will have a power capacity of [q1: 1 GW] and an energy storage capacity of [q2: 2 GWh], with Matrix Renewables retaining a majority stake in each project. Once operational, the storage is expected to equal the annual electricity consumption of approximately [q4: 520,000 households]. The partnership aims to create or support more than [q3: 200 jobs] across construction and operations phases.
items.title: National Wealth Fund and Matrix Renewables partner on 1 GW battery storage projects in Scotland.

items.summary: The Solar Energy Corporation of India Limited (SECI), a Navratna under the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy, issued on November 20, 2026 a single-stage, double-envelope e-tender for Indian power trading licensees to trade renewable energy across its approximately 65.8 GW portfolio. SECI holds long-term Power Sale Agreements with distribution utilities and traded around 62 billion units during FY 2025-26; selected partners would support selling untied capacity, projects with delayed or unstarted offtake, SECI-owned renewable energy and storage assets, and jointly developed projects. Eligible bidders must be Indian-incorporated companies holding a valid Category-I, II or III inter-State trading licence issued by the CERC—joint ventures, consortiums and LLPs are excluded—and must show an average annual power trading volume of at least 4,000 million units across FY 2023-24 to FY 2025-26 plus an average annual turnover of at least ₹422 crore with positive net worth. Technical qualification is scored on trading volume, turnover and credit rating (at least 60 out of 100 marks), with technical evaluation weighted at 75% and financial bids at 25%; financially qualified applicants are then selected via Quality Cum Cost Based Selection. Bidders must submit an EMD of ₹12 lakh and a Performance Security Deposit of ₹60 lakh within 15 days of the Letter of Award, pay a non-refundable processing fee of ₹25,000 plus GST (waived for eligible micro and small enterprises with UDYAM registration), keep bids valid for 180 days, acknowledge the award within seven days and execute the contract within 30 days. The proposal is forward-looking: it sets tender terms and eligibility thresholds rather than reporting completed trading outcomes.
items.title: SECI invites bids to manage renewable energy trading across its 65.8 GW portfolio

visual.alt: Bar chart. lakh 12 ₹; Performance Security Deposit 60 ₹; non-refundable processing fee 25,000 ₹.

items.summary: The document's substantive claim, attributed to its headline, is that the Senate just passed permitting reform. However, this text provides no supporting evidence for that legislative outcome—no vote count, bill number, sponsor, or passage details—and instead consists entirely of a subscription and membership sales pitch from Heatmap (a paywall notice offering unlimited access, virtual briefings, events; an upsell tier with exclusive polling and VIP reception tickets), plus login prompts. No figures, dates, or quotable statements about the permitting reform itself are present in the source.
items.title: Senate passed permitting reform; Heatmap content is paywalled

items.summary: The Reserve Bank of India clarified that Indian residents earning services income from overseas clients—such as content writers, graphic designers, software developers, consultants, and digital marketers—are no longer required to file a separate Export Declaration Form (EDF) when their authorized bank receives the necessary payment details; submitting that information is treated as EDF filing. RBI stated there is no maximum ceiling on this exemption for individual service exporters, so even payments above ₹10 lakh are covered, illustrated by an example of a freelancer receiving ₹12 lakh from a foreign client without separate filing. However, RBI specified that companies, partnership firms, and other commercial entities remain subject to the rule requiring EDF when a single foreign payment equals or exceeds ₹10 lakh in foreign currency terms. The clarification falls under new foreign trade rules effective October 1, 2026; transactions begun before that date retain prior regulations, though invoices issued on or before October 1 with payments received from that date onward fall under the exemption. RBI also noted authorized banks gained authority to approve certain older transactions previously reserved for RBI. Freelancers still must provide payment details—sender information, service type, amount, and transaction purpose—to their bank, which may request supporting documents such as invoices or contracts; compliance with banking, foreign exchange, and income tax rules remains unchanged.
items.title: RBI exempts individual freelancers from separate EDF filing on foreign service payments of any amount; corporate entities still required to file when a single payment equals or exceeds ₹10 lakh, effective under new rules from October 1, 2026.

items.summary: Levent Alpöge, an Anthropic employee and mathematician, claimed on November 20 that he spent approximately six weeks working with the company's AI chatbot Claude to develop a proof of the Riemann hypothesis. The claim remains unverified; it is presented as an assertion by Alpöge rather than an independently confirmed result, though if true it could represent a historic development for both mathematics and artificial intelligence. The announcement followed Anthropic's US stock market debut on November 19, adding to the company's profile in the AI industry. No numerical comparison or chart data is available.
items.title: Anthropic mathematician claims Claude helped prove Riemann hypothesis

items.summary: The article frames UK inflation as an 'invisible stealth tax' on savings: with inflation at [q3: 3.6%] in October and the Bank of England expecting it to rise further to about [q4: 5%] by mid-2027, savers lose real value when their interest rate is below that level. Beating inflation depends on tax status—non-taxpayers or Isa holders only need a rate above [q5: 3.6%], whereas a basic-rate taxpayer must earn [q7: 4.5%] and a higher-rate taxpayer [q8: 6%] just to match it. Moneyfacts reports there are now more than [q13: 1,649 available] savings accounts exceeding the inflation threshold if no tax applies, including [q15: 879 fixed-rate] bonds (best-buy rates from [q16: 4.67%] on a six-month GB Bank bond to [q17: 5.37%] on a five-year StreamBank bond) and [q18: 130 easy access] accounts, plus more than [q21: 400 fixed-rate] cash Isas (top payers UBL UK at [q23: 5.3%] and Shawbrook Bank at [q24: 5.27%], both requiring five-year terms; easy-access Chip and Moneybox apps offer initial rates of [q25: 4.87%] and [q26: 4.86%]). A worked example shows that on a £10,000 balance over one year at inflation of [q27: 3.6%], a bond paying [q29: 5.21%] returns gross interest of [q30: £521] but only real value of [q31: £161]; the same sum in an account paying [q32: 2%] yields £[q33: 200] interest yet leaves the saver worse off by [q34: £160] after inflation. The piece also notes escalating annuities (set increases of [q37: 3%] or [q38: 5%], or index-linked to RPI, which was [q39: 4.2%] in October) and index-linked gilts as ways to protect spending power, while cautioning that gilt prices are sensitive to interest-rate moves.
items.title: UK inflation at 3.6% in October; Bank of England expects it to rise to ~5% by mid-2027, eroding savings unless rates exceed the post-tax threshold

visual.alt: Bar chart. rate 3.6 %; earn 4.5 %; higher-rate taxpayer 6 %.

items.summary: The Emergent Ventures program announced its 60th cohort, a group of early-stage founders—mostly teenagers and young adults from cities including Abu Dhabi, Helsinki, London area, Warsaw area, Istanbul, Samsun (Turkey), Izmir, Hermosa Beach, Stanford, Harvard, and Eleutheros Tech—who are working on AI models, AI agents, energy information for the UK, organ-transplant genetics, trucking logistics, nuclear fusion, longevity research, on-device AI, an AI companion, an economics-learning site with agents, superior connectivity for the UK, science/AI/space work. The list presents each founder's name, location, age where given (13, 15, 16, 17, or 18), and focus area; it does not report funding amounts, valuations, or program outcomes beyond cohort membership.
items.title: Emergent Ventures 60th cohort: young founders across Europe

items.summary: On Friday (Nov 20), Bitcoin slid to $55,830 by 11:13 p.m. ET on Saturday at 0413 GMT, down 5.10 per cent—the lowest since September 2024—after earlier falling below $60,000 for the first time since July and dropping 3.57 per cent to $56,813.68. The decline was attributed to concerns over stretched valuations in AI stocks, alongside rising borrowing costs, regulatory risks following Democrats' win in the US midterm elections, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's departure, and worries about profitability of massive AI infrastructure spending; meanwhile main US stock indexes were on track for their steepest weekly decline since April 2025.
items.title: Bitcoin fell to its lowest level in two years amid AI-stock and risk-asset worries.

items.summary: The Information reported that SoftBank Group CEO Masayoshi Son had approached Wall Street institutions to finance a possible trillion-dollar acquisition of South Korean memory chipmaker SK Hynix, citing people familiar with the matter. A SoftBank spokesperson then told The Information the deal was no longer under active consideration, saying "SoftBank explores many opportunities, and this one is no longer under active consideration." SK Hynix stated it had no knowledge of the reported transaction and noted that any foreign acquisition would require prior government approval under Korean law. All figures are attributed to The Information's reporting; SoftBank and SK Hynix did not independently confirm the buyout discussion.
items.title: SoftBank reportedly dropped trillion-dollar SK Hynix buyout

items.summary: A New England co-op of about [q5: 200] fishers is challenging the view that offshore wind and commercial fishing are natural enemies by training scallopers—boats legally restricted to fewer than 36 days a year—to support construction, paying each vessel $[q6: 4.5 thousand] a day plus fuel; Sea Services says it has paid out [q8: 34 million dollars] total across several windfarms and that the work also supports onshore trades in New Bedford, where the port generates about [q10: 300 million dollars] annually but runs with a deficit. Founded by Gary Yerman in [d2: 2020], after he visited fishers working offshore wind in Northern Ireland in [d3: 2019], the model gained traction partly because scallopers sought extra income during pandemic-driven seafood demand drops; Capt Jack Morris joined Sea Services in [d4: 2021]. The co-op's benefits may be short-lived, however: after courts rejected a January [d1: 2025] executive order halting five east coast projects, the administration shifted to spending nearly [q9: 4 billion dollars] buying back wind leases, chilling developer investment and drying up Sea Services work. Capt Kevin Souza said his shifts have stretched from roughly three days off per cycle to ten between shifts; CEO Gordon Videll noted that even completed projects will take years of construction before the industry recovers.
items.title: Sea Services fishers earn a second income from offshore wind as Trump administration works to end new projects.

items.summary: Anthropic closed at $88.91 on Friday, 8.5% below Thursday's close and near its $83 IPO price, underscoring that even the first large machine-learning model maker to go public could not lift a sector weighed down by broader tech declines.
items.title: Anthropic's IPO fell short as AI trade selloff continued

visual.alt: Bar chart. closed 88.91 $; s close and not far 83 $.

items.summary: Chinese Premier Li Qiang and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, meeting at the 11th China-Australia Annual Leaders' Meeting in Beijing on November 20, 2026, reaffirmed commitment to eliminating disruptions to economic and trade exchanges. Li framed their remarks within a broader claim that bilateral cooperation has made 'considerable new progress over the past year,' attributing this to complementary economic strengths rather than citing specific measurable outcomes. He proposed three priority areas—consumption upgrading in tourism, education, healthcare, biomedicine and high-end medical services; innovation cooperation in digital and intelligent technologies; and green low-carbon transition through green steel supply chains and new energy vehicle industrial chains—but presented these as forward-looking proposals without reported progress or quantified results. Albanese echoed the sentiment, noting China is Australia's largest trading partner and pointing to 2027 as the 55th anniversary of diplomatic relations established in 1972; he cited artificial intelligence, green transition and modern agriculture as future cooperation areas but offered no current figures on trade volumes or sectoral performance. Both leaders' statements are assertions of intent rather than reports of measurable economic outcomes.
items.title: China-Australia leaders pledge stable business ties amid global trade uncertainty

items.summary: A promotional piece on octopus fishing in Lanshan, eastern Shandong Province presents the activity as accessible to anyone with proper equipment and knowledge of tides and weather. The text attributes abundant fresh seafood supply to a healthy marine environment but offers no supporting data or verification for these claims.
items.title: Octopus fishing promoted as recreation off Lanshan, Shandong

items.summary: Following four men's convictions in Joanne Young's case, campaigners and legal figures have called for public debate over how the law treats third-party consent. Philip Young pleaded guilty to abusing his wife by sedating her into an unconscious state before inviting strangers who then sexually abused her; she waived anonymity after he advertised her on dating websites as a 'kink.' Joanne Young said no one should be able to give consent on another's behalf, and daughter Alex Young echoed this. Barrister Kate Parker of the Schools Consent Project noted there is no law permitting third-party consent as a defence under the Sexual Offences Act 2003, though defendants relied on genuinely believing she was consenting; Harriet Wistrich of the Centre for Women's Justice said juries should reject such myths and explicitly clarify that someone cannot consent on another's behalf. Ciara Bergman of Rape Crisis England & Wales stressed existing law already requires genuine choice with freedom and capacity to make it, arguing the problem lies in misinterpretation rather than statute; Prof Miranda Horvath emphasized legally nobody can give consent on your behalf and called for clear education from young people through adults. Labour MP Jess Phillips urged the government to strengthen-test whether third-party consent can never be asserted in law, suggesting tighter laws might have spared Young her trial. A Ministry of Justice spokesperson reaffirmed that no one can consent on someone else's behalf and said criminal law is kept under review.
items.title: Campaigners back call for scrutiny of consent laws after drug-facilitated rape trial

items.summary: Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told the BBC that a UK-EU agreement reached on Friday will enter force whether or not the two sides reach a separate arrangement over EU students' tuition fees. The measures include scrapping most checks on British food exports in return for the UK adopting some EU regulations from [d1: 2028], plus a new youth mobility scheme, and Miliband said these would apply even without a tuition deal because President Ursula von der Leyen described them as distinct agreements rather than one document. European Commission President von der Leyen expressed confidence that a solution to the fees issue could be found, with Prime Minister Andy Burnham adding he agreed during the press conference announcing the agreement. The prime minister said the Treasury believes the cooperation deal could boost the UK economy by up to [q1: £17bn] a year and lower living costs while reducing red tape, though Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch disputed this figure as unfounded and cited modelling putting the economic benefit at [q3: 0.0%]. When asked whether rejoining the EU would be considered, Miliband said all options remain on the table even after accepting the result of the [d2: 2016] Brexit referendum, noting that both Britain and Europe have changed significantly since then.
items.title: UK-EU cooperation deal to take effect regardless of tuition fees outcome, Miliband says

items.summary: The Financial Services Authority (OJK) announced sanctions across 10 capital market violation cases, returning Rp23.77 billion (~US$1.3 million) in illicit gains from three stock manipulation cases involving PT Grand House Mulia, PT Saraswanti Anugerah Makmur and PT Suryamas Dutamakmur, while imposing a total of Rp3.71 billion in administrative fines on seven listed companies for disclosure failures, material and affiliated-party transaction breaches, financial reporting violations and non-compliance with share transfer obligations; OJK also barred multiple individuals from capital markets, derivatives and carbon exchange sectors for three to 10 years, citing broader efforts to strengthen enforcement amid prior concerns over transparency raised by global index providers.
items.title: Indonesia's OJK sanctioned 10 capital market violations with returns and fines

visual.alt: Bar chart. ordered the return 23,770,000,000 rupiah; agency also imposed a total 3,710,000,000 rupiah.

items.summary: Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky labelled Vladimir Putin a "killer" in response to Donald Trump calling the Russian leader his "friend" during a trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping. Speaking to CNN, Zelensky said it was up to Trump how to describe Putin but that for Ukraine he is an enemy and someone who kills each day and night; he added that treating Putin as a friend means Russia feels insufficient pressure. The exchange followed Russian attacks on Friday that killed at least nine people in strikes targeting bridges in Kyiv and railway stations, which Zelensky called the biggest attack of the year after Ukraine damaged the Crimean Bridge. He said Ukraine endured civilian deaths and injuries from an onslaught of 110 missiles, including 27 ballistic, and more than 400 drones. Hours later Trump told reporters that Putin would love to end the war because both Zelensky and Putin want peace. Separately, Poland reported a Russian cruise missile among three objects violating its airspace in the southeast early Friday during Western military exercises; Prime Minister Donald Tusk called it a provocation with no injuries or damage, while Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned the violations after jets were scrambled.
items.title: Zelensky calls Putin a 'killer' after Trump's friendship remark

items.summary: Russian ballistic missile and drone strikes have damaged several of Kyiv's road bridges since early October, restricting the Northern Bridge to buses while limiting other crossings. A marshrutka driver crossing the damaged bridge up to [q1: 24] times a day (down from as many as [q2: 20]) said it would take “a huge number of missiles” to destroy one and that its supporting structures remained unscathed, with holes later covered over. Transport expert Dmytro Bespalov noted suspension bridges are strong and repairable but warned Kyiv is strategically vulnerable because the city had few pre-war bridges—ranking third in Europe for congestion on the TomTom traffic index as of [d1: 2021], behind Istanbul and Moscow—and that planned floating pontoon replacements could bear far less load, requiring [q5: 20] to equal half current capacity while being more vulnerable to attack. Residents expressed resilience amid electricity shortages and lack of heating; one construction worker said if the bridges were destroyed he would move with his wife to relatives' house across the river.
items.title: Kyiv residents unbothered by Russian attacks on city's bridges

items.summary: The Indian Youth Congress stormed Meta offices in Hyderabad on Friday (Nov [d1: 20]), smashing plants and clashing with police after Instagram accounts of its members were removed; workers also spray-painted anti-Meta slogans outside Mumbai's office and held banners demanding restoration of youth group accounts. Two such accounts were restored, but thousands of journalist, creator, and influencer accounts critical of the government remain restricted, per Manu Jain of the youth group, who said Meta must explain its algorithmic restrictions and restore government-ordered takedowns. Congress accuses platforms of curbing dissent while Modi's government says it orders removals only for breaches of local law or threats to public safety; Rulers Without Borders notes rising removal of journalistic content in India this year amid a February rule requiring takedown within three hours, down from 36.
items.title: Meta restricted more than 5.4 million posts or accounts in India under local laws in H1 2026, second only to Indonesia and up from about 70,000 the prior six months.

items.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy branded Vladimir Putin a "killer" in response to Donald Trump calling the Russian leader his "friend," warning that such descriptions could ease pressure on Putin. The remarks followed Trump describing his relationships with both Putin and Xi Jinping as fantastic, while also noting that both Zelenskyy and Putin wanted to end the war but "don't know how." Zelenskyy told CNN: "For us, he is an enemy... for us, he is a killer," adding that most people in the world see him as such. The exchange came after Russian forces launched what Zelenskyy called one of the largest attacks of the war from Thursday night into Friday morning, firing more than 400 attack drones and over 110 missiles—striking civilian infrastructure including energy facilities, bridges across the Dnipro River, and railway lines that killed at least seven people in Kyiv. The assault followed Putin's warning of no negotiations on a partial ceasefire after Ukrainian strikes destroyed part of his prized Crimea bridge.
items.title: Zelenskyy calls Putin a 'killer' after Trump's friendship remark

items.summary: The article argues that Australian cricket's senior bowlers have damaged their own and Australia's credibility not primarily through what happened in [d1: 2018] — which most fans no longer believe or care about — but through a self-absorbed culture of entitlement and narrative control, exemplified by Josh Hazlewood threatening to review his place if Pat Cummins lost the captaincy. Former wicketkeeper Ian Healy is quoted as saying Australia's bowlers are 'not as credible as they once were,' distinguishing this from their performance legacies. The author contends that even a disastrous tour of South Africa, which featured Scott Boland being dropped for Nathan Lyon in favor of Simon Harmer — who publicly dismantled the captain — proved a deeper crisis than any setback framing suggested. In the time since Sandpapergate, Cricket Australia has had six chairmen, four CEOs, three men's head coaches and capped [q2: 21 new] Test players, yet mainstays have attained over-mighty status. Players' union boss Paul Marsh is quoted as admitting there was 'decreasing' support among players for the idea of Test cricket as the pinnacle of the sport. These are attributed claims by a single columnist rather than established facts; no numerical comparison between the 2018 event and current perceptions is provided, so comparable readings are unavailable.
items.title: Australian bowlers' public credibility is being eroded more by a self-appointed culture of entitlement than by the original 2018 scandal, according to ABC Sport columnist.

items.summary: At the 2026 APEC CEO Summit in Shenzhen, China proposed creating a global economic cooperation association linking major world-class bay areas to expand collaboration on innovation, trade and shared challenges across the Asia-Pacific. The proposal frames four recognized regions—the San Francisco Bay Area (technology and venture capital), New York (finance and professional services), Tokyo (advanced manufacturing with technological capabilities) and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area (manufacturing, trade, shipping and innovation)—as complementary economies whose distinct strengths could drive shared growth. The initiative follows a 10-point plan released at the 2026 Global Bay Area Economic Forum in Guangzhou calling for greater openness, improved shipping connectivity and better coordination of rules, and aligns with San Francisco Bay Area Council's Jennifer Zou, who said her region and the GBA should deepen cooperation in health care, artificial intelligence safety and climate change. The proposal is a stated plan rather than an established outcome; experts such as Liaoning University president Yu Miaojie say closer ties could expand collective economic strength and advance sustainable development worldwide.
items.title: China proposes global bay-area trade association

items.summary: While President Donald Trump centered this week's Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders' summit on great-power realignment, two U.S. allies advanced their own bilateral tracks: Canada opened a channel with Beijing, while Japan—already at odds with China—turned to partners elsewhere in Asia. This middle-power diplomacy was overshadowed Thursday when Trump met Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin at a lakeside villa in Shenzhen, an event that dominated the summit. Trump characterized the meeting as 'bigger than Yalta,' referencing the 1945 conference at which the United States, Britain, and the Soviet Union divided up postwar Europe—a comparison he made without independent verification.
items.title: Middle powers pursue independent diplomacy as Trump hosts Xi and Putin

items.summary: An unusually early sudden stratospheric warming event flipped the polar vortex, and forecasters warn it heightens the odds of colder temperatures, more storms, wind and heating demand across Europe over the next month—though analysts caution a single SSW is short-term and would need to be repeated for sustained winter effect. The cold comes as EU gas stocks hit record lows, prompting warnings that consumption may have to be cut by seven per cent this winter; reserves are being squeezed by war-driven disruption of LNG shipping ahead of a full ban on Russian LNG imports from January 2027. Separately, the European Heat Pump Association reported in June that Europe's heat pumps provide as much heat as the LNG carried by more than [q5: 200 tankers], which is double what arrived from the Middle East and around seven per cent of total annual imported LNG—avoiding €9.7 billion in import costs last year—and new research suggests air-source heat pumps could help heat a home on a typical winter day for as little as [q7: £1.84] (approximately [q8: €2.20]) when used effectively, though Montel's Jean-Paul Harreman noted that high electricity prices during the worst cold could still raise costs even if efficiency beats gas boilers over an annual total.
items.title: Europe braces for a cold winter as an early polar vortex flip strains gas supplies while heat pumps are pitched as energy-security relief

items.summary: An article by Gu Baojing of Zhejiang University argues that COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye on November 19, 2026 should focus on turning climate targets into deliverable policy rather than conference talk. A proposal discussed there would raise electricity's share of global final energy consumption to [q2: 35%] by [d2: 2035], but the author stresses that emissions cuts depend not just on electrification itself—cleaner power generation, stronger grids and storage must advance together—or replacing equipment alone leaves much unrealized. The piece also flags methane and other non-carbon-dioxide greenhouse gases as needing action across agriculture, waste and land management. On finance, it notes the African Group's insistence that climate funding must not deepen debt burdens, warning that expensive loans can crowd out spending on disaster preparedness even if headline amounts grow. A fair transition is framed around who bears costs and shares benefits—workers in coal regions, small farmers and low-income households—with neglect risking political backlash. The author concludes COP31 should aim for emissions ambition backed by finance at a pace societies can sustain, with credibility resting on visible improvements beyond the conference hall.
items.title: COP31 tests whether climate promises become affordable action

items.summary: David Koppel, now 65 and retired from paparazzi work, recounts the incidents in his new 300-page memoir Spotlight (q1) covering what he calls his ‘golden decade’ (d2: 1986 to d3: 1997), when he pursued Britain’s biggest stars. The book centers on defiance and access—his unauthorized shot of Mick Jagger sticking out his tongue while being punched, a smuggled camera at the 1991 Stepping Out premiere (d4) that netted an exclusive photo of Diana greeting Liza Minnelli, and punches from David Bowie in 1987 (d6) and Bob Dylan with a newspaper in 1993 (d5). Koppel attributes his continued success to chasing subjects before PR control made modern fame ‘staged’ and celebrities lacking the depth or class of figures like Michael Caine and Paul McCartney. The economic basis for this work has eroded sharply: he charged £402.50 (£q2, €q3) for an Elton John photo and £460 (€q4) for Andrew Lloyd Webber in 1990 (d7), earned up to £5,000 (almost €q5) for a Pierce Brosnan shot, and was paid £10,000 (£q6) for an unremarkable TV-series photo—sums he says newspapers no longer pay. To produce the memoir he scanned 5,000 negatives (q7), narrowed them to 1,200 photos (q8), then selected 250 (q9). The work complements his earlier book Limelight and continues alongside ventures like Pap Art, founded in 2004 (d10); the memoir’s value rests on Koppel’s testimony rather than independently verified claims.
items.title: Paparazzo David Koppel’s memoir frames his golden decade of celebrity chases amid a photography market that has since collapsed

items.summary: In an EL PAÍS interview conducted in a Manhattan café, George Saunders focuses on Un baño en una laguna mientras llueve (A Swim in a Pond in the Rain), recently released by Capitán Swing. The book originated from 20 years of teaching a narrative course on short stories at Syracuse University; after being told his class would no longer be offered, he transcribed and refined his notes over three years to create a collection analyzing works by Russian masters including Chekhov, whose title alludes to the climactic scene in “Gooseberrys.” Saunders expresses surprise that it became an unusual bestseller for such a work, noting it sells even more now than at first release. He explains he does not fully understand why readers connect with it but attributes this to its frankness and teaching quality, especially for those who cannot access MFA programs or lack exposure to short stories. On whether creative writing can be taught, he says instructors guide rather than teach writing directly, helping students find their own voice through line editing and structural reconsideration; the book instead offers a “ramp” toward understanding that a story is compressed art distinct from real life. He describes the most magical quality of great short stories as an understory rising to reveal meaning only late in the narrative when the writer’s epiphany occurs, paralleling James Joyce’s “The Dead.” This analytical approach also drove his Substack Story Club with George Saunders, which he built by posting weekly story analyses and opening comments for discussion. The interview notes that Saunders won the Booker Prize in 2017 for Lincoln in the Bardo, whose opera premiere at the MET occurred two weeks before this conversation.
items.title: George Saunders discusses his Spanish-translated short story book and its unexpected success

items.summary: Convicted former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro, serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest over a coup attempt and aged 71, was taken to DF Star Hospital in Brasília on Friday with abdominal pain. His son Carlos reported that the former leader had been found to have 'a near-complete intestinal obstruction,' while the hospital described him as suffering from 'abdominal distension.' An initial medical response involved medication for pain and an attempt to reverse the condition without invasive intervention, according to Carlos. Bolsonaro was in power from 2019 to 2022 before losing the 2022 election to Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva; he was convicted last year of plotting a coup and claims his imprisonment is 'a left-wing judicial witch hunt.' Carlos blamed house arrest for his father's health problems, stating that Bolsonaro's condition had been 'deteriorating every day in prison due to his lack of mobility' alongside what he called 'the psychological torture he suffers daily.'
items.title: Bolsonaro hospitalized for intestinal obstruction

items.summary: On Nov. 6 a high-intensity downpour flooded parts of Colombo, stranding commuters and submerging vehicles; meteorological readings put the rate at more than [q9: 120 mm] ([q10: 4.7 in]) per hour at one gauge and more than [q11: 135 mm] ([q12: 5.3 in]) per hour elsewhere, while CMC's storm water system was designed to withhold only [q14: 30 mm] ([q15: 1.18 in]) per hour and officials cited rainfall exceeding [q16: 100 mm] [[q17: 3.9] in] per hour on that day, so the system was overwhelmed (Ajith Wijemanna, director of Sri Lanka's Department of Meteorology; Deepika Wijethilake, deputy director engineering at CMC). The event prompted PM Harini Amarasuriya to order canal and drainage cleaning, after which authorities identified [q13: 60 key] locations with blocked drains. Officials attribute the flooding chiefly to rainfall intensity rather than total volume, noting historical totals such as [q5: 493.7 mm] ([q6: 19.4 in]) in June [d1: 1992] and [q7: 440.2 mm] ([q8: 17.3 in]) over 24 hours in November [d2: 2010], both exceeding the Nov. 6 total of [q1: 129]-millimeter ([q2: 5]-inch). Sri Lanka lacks an operational Doppler radar, so accurate forecasts with lead time are not possible; once installed, officials say it would enable better prediction. Colombo's wetlands—37% of incoming rainwater is retained by the complex but only around [q21: 20 square] kilometers ([q22: 7.7 square] miles) remain—are degraded by urbanization and invasive species like pond apple, reducing absorption capacity (Chethika Gunasiri). A 2025 study links real estate development to wetland loss and property price spikes of about [q18: 30]-40% around Kaduwela, Malabe and Thalawathugoda; CSF's Anushka Wijesinha argues for valuing wetlands' economic worth—citing a 2003 study—and warns that over [q19: 45%] of the country's GDP comes from the Western Province. Proposed solutions include Copenhagen-style rain gardens and bioswales, CMC plans to design systems withholding more than [q23: 100 mm] ([q24: 3.9 in]) per hour, and an 'adaptation and resilience fund' blending government money, grants, development bank funds, philanthropy, and fees on property developers.
items.title: Colombo flash flood exposed by rainfall intensity exceeding century-old drainage capacity

items.summary: This morning briefing reports a cluster of international developments, led by US President Donald Trump threatening military action against Iran over a rumored 'dirty bomb' plot targeting Washington. Trump said: "If they do (that), we're going to fight," insisting his administration is closely monitoring Tehran and had extensive intelligence on its activities; Iranian authorities denied Friday reports of a US-Israeli missile strike on Qeshm Island, attributing explosions to disposal of unexploded munitions from previous attacks. Separately, Denmark ordered the Russian defense attache to leave within seven days and will halt non-essential visas for Russian citizens, with Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen calling it "enough is enough" while noting Denmark would not expel all Russian diplomats; Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said Danish authorities linked a foiled assassination plot targeting a US-Ukrainian citizen to Russian intelligence services. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz called for a '360-degree partnership' with Qatar, welcoming its pledge to invest an additional €15 billion ($16.5 billion) in Germany and praising its mediation efforts between the parties to the conflict; Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani described Germany as an important partner and urged de-escalation. Trump also downplayed a wave of banking, technology, and service outages across the country, attributing many to companies upgrading their systems and saying "they're all separate events," while blaming air traffic control disruptions on infrastructure that is '55 years old and older' and said his administration is seeking $50 billion from Congress to build a new system. The briefing also covers numerous other items: Education Cannot Wait announced $52 million for more than 300,000 children affected by crises in Lebanon, Myanmar, and South Sudan; Palestinian prisoner groups reported 350 Palestinian children held in Israeli prisons with more than 2,000 child arrests since October 2023; a magnitude 6.7 earthquake struck near Ondores in Peru's Junin region at roughly 82 miles depth; an early trial of daraxonrasib shrank tumors in 60.7% of 61 patients with advanced pancreatic cancer; the US held its first offshore critical minerals lease sale off American Samoa drawing $6 million from a sole bidder despite a voided environmental clearance ruling; Japan agreed to buy up to 8 million barrels of Saudi crude while gaining temporary storage for 16 million barrels; Lufthansa plans to cut 1,000 full-time jobs after posting €180 million operating loss in the first nine months of 2026; Angola's Endiama will pay $180 million for a 10% stake in De Beers; UEFA fined England's Football Association €15,000 ($17,300) and imposed a suspended ban after supporters' anti-Catholic and anti-Irish chanting during the 3-2 win over Spain; FIA will introduce full-time stewards to Formula 1 in 2027 with a long-term goal of 12 to 15 officials; more than 20,000 people signed a petition against Marilyn Manson at Slipknot's July 3, 2027 Wembley show amid abuse allegations; Christie's withdrew Frida Kahlo's 1952 painting estimated at $2.5 million to $3.5 million after Mexican authorities requested provenance information; the European-Japanese BepiColombo mission is set to enter orbit around Mercury after an eight-year journey covering nearly 10 billion kilometers (6.2 billion miles), with scientific operations beginning April 2027 and separation from its Japanese counterpart Mio scheduled Dec. 9-10; Signal announced it is restricting screenshots on iOS 27 and screen capture by AI assistants on Android to protect privacy, though the company warned disabling these measures could expose messages to AI systems.
items.title: Trump threatens military action over rumored Iran dirty bomb plot; Denmark expels Russian defense attache

items.summary: Police in US cities posted tongue-in-cheek social-media warnings as Grand Theft Auto VI's launch hype peaked, reminding fans that car theft, street racing, reckless driving, and violence remain illegal off-screen. The Atlanta Police Department said "GTA is not a real place, but Atlanta is!" urging residents to keep virtual entertainment separate from real-life decisions; Aurora, Colorado police joked about the game's six-star wanted system versus one star earning handcuffs in reality; Denver told players "Playing GTA 6 from your couch is highly encouraged," while Port St. Lucie and San Juan, Texas departments likewise framed fictional crimes as confined to the game. The warnings coincided with Rockstar Games' global release of GTA VI on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S, its first mainline installment since Grand Theft Auto V in [d3: 2013]. Analytics platform Sensor Tower estimated $[q5] revenue from pre-orders and launch-day sales, citing 24.58 million copies sold by late Thursday; Rockstar Games and Take-Two Interactive had not yet released official figures but described demand as "unprecedented." The police statements are promotional-style reminders rather than new legislation or enforcement actions.
items.title: US police departments urge players to keep GTA VI crimes inside video game

items.summary: Scientists led by Tilo Nadler have proposed a new-to-science primate—the short-tailed langur (Trachypithecus brevicaudus)—from the Annamite Mountains of Laos based solely on photographs showing tails noticeably shorter and thicker than related limestone langurs such as the Lao langur (Trachypithecus laotum) and Hatinh langur (T. hatinhensis). Nadler, lead author of a 2026 paper in the Vietnamese Journal of Primatology, says the encounter revealed an entire population rather than a single tail-injured individual. However, primate expert Vincent Nijman, who was not involved with the study, argues the data do not yet support declaring a distinct species: he notes that Hatinh langurs have tails as short as those of the proposed new species at its longest, and that thickness could not be quantified. Nadler acknowledges there is no body or genetic evidence; his team previously failed to find remains in villages but plans future expeditions to search more thoroughly and collect droppings for DNA analysis. The animal was first photographed by Rob Timmins of the Saola Foundation in 2024, though that group says it was not involved with Nadler's research.
items.title: A proposed new Laos langur species rests on photos alone, drawing skepticism over insufficient evidence.

items.summary: Republican Sen. Ron Johnson of Wisconsin, who chairs the Senate Budget Committee and has defended President Trump's conflict with Iran, said Friday he opposes conditioning government funding on ending the war as Congress approaches a Dec. 11 deadline to keep federal agencies operating before Christmas. He stated that shutting down the war is "President Trump's power" exercised under his constitutional authority (Morning Edition). Johnson preferred bipartisan negotiations over budget reconciliation, which could let Republicans approve defense funding without Democratic support; he said Republicans would give Democrats one more chance at talks before the Thanksgiving recess. A shutdown risks furloughing hundreds of thousands of federal workers or delaying their pay just weeks before Christmas, and Johnson warned temporary spending measures would hinder military modernization and weapons procurement, citing changing warfare in Ukraine as an example. He also expressed that he hopes Iranians rise up against their government and that Iran never acquires a nuclear weapon (Morning Edition).
items.title: GOP Sen. Johnson rejects tying government funding to an end to the Iran war

items.summary: The International Court of Justice ruled on Thursday that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya in 2016 and 2017, its first-ever finding of genocide against a state. The court rejected Myanmar's counterinsurgency defense as "far in excess of what was justified by military necessity," per ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa reading from the panel's 9-6 decision. It ordered preventive measures, legal reforms, and victim reparations or compensation within two years, plus safe return and prosecution—but enforcement depends on the UN Security Council, where China and Russia would likely veto any punitive resolution. A UN fact-finding mission concluded roughly 10,000 people died in the pogroms, with about 1 in 5 being children. Rohingya activists welcomed the verdict as validation but warned it will not stop ongoing violence or enable return while military leader Min Aung Hlaing remains in power amid civil war and continued persecution by the Arakan Army.
items.title: ICJ rules Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya; remedies face enforcement wall

items.summary: Nvidia shares dropped [q1: 46%] over the past seven weeks, erasing approximately [q2: $2.6 trillion] in market value per Reuters; this figure is attributed to an unverified source and represents the article's claim rather than established fact. The decline pushed Nvidia from the world's most valuable company to fourth place behind Apple, Microsoft, and Alphabet. Co-founder Jensen Huang resigned on November 12 amid reports of extramarital relationships, including one with a Chinese businesswoman allegedly suspected of being a spy; he has agreed to testify before the Senate (date unspecified) and give a closed-door interview to three House committees on December 1. Interim CEO Colette Kress projected [q5: 75%] revenue growth for fiscal year [d2: 2028], though this is an interim projection rather than a confirmed result. The selloff began before the leadership crisis, driven by concerns over AI-spending sustainability and competition from Google and AMD; it continued despite better-than-expected earnings and raised guidance. Nvidia's valuation fell to around [q6: 8.4 times] forward earnings versus [q7: 29 times] for AMD on projected profits—these are reported figures, not independently verified valuations. The broader market declined Friday as the S&P 500 and Dow confirmed corrections after falling more than [q9: 10%] from record highs; the Nasdaq plunged [q10: 5.28%] to 22,617.73 while the S&P dropped [q12: 3.70%] to 6,910.42 and the Dow fell [q14: 1.93%] to 48,147.33—these are reported closing readings attributed to an unverified source.
items.title: Nvidia's stock fell 46% over seven weeks as leadership turmoil and AI-spending doubts drove a broad tech selloff.

visual.alt: Bar chart. stock trading 8.4 time; compared 29 time.

items.summary: Allegations dating back nearly two decades that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang verbally abused employees, threatened them and made sexually explicit remarks have resurfaced amid questions over his leadership following his resignation this month. The claims originate from a 2007 lawsuit cited by Bloomberg court documents, brought by Stephen Pettigrew, the company's first in-house lawyer who joined in September [d2: 1999] and was dismissed in June [d3: 2006], alleging he was fired after flagging executive conduct. In his filing, Pettigrew claimed Huang would 'scream at them, threaten them with extreme bodily harm and make sexually oriented comments while thrusting his hips in a demonstration of the sex act.' The lawsuit sought more than [q1: $2.6 million] in damages before being resolved through a confidential settlement in December [d4: 2009]. A second former employee, Michael Winston, Nvidia's senior vice president for human resources who joined in September [d6: 2004], filed a discrimination complaint in [d5: 2005] alleging dismissal after objecting to Huang's abusive treatment of employees; Nvidia settled with him confidentially for more than [q2: $1 million]. Both men are now dead. The allegations resurface as Huang faces scrutiny over his demanding management style, which he has described as 'torturing' those working closely with him, and amid disclosures about alleged affairs that prompted his resignation. A representative rejected the claims, calling them false and more than 20 years old; Nvidia did not comment. All reported allegations were made in legal proceedings and were never established as court findings.
items.title: Nvidia ex-HR's allegations against Jensen Huang resurface amid leadership uncertainty

items.summary: Mathematician Levent Alpöge says he believes he has found a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, an 1859 conjecture and one of seven Millennium Prize Problems chosen in [d1: 2000], developed with assistance from Anthropic's Claude model. He posted the work on his website in Lean, describing the AI-generated version as more than [q1: 250,000 pages] and an unreadable travesty; he called it "incredibly long." The proof has not been formally accepted by mathematicians, who are still reviewing whether the reasoning holds. Alpöge said the result came late Sunday into Monday, days before Anthropic's public market debut, which he called timing that was "horrible," and messaged CEO Dario Amodei to ask permission to announce it; Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment after his post, as its stock fell [q2: 13.04%] on its first full day of trading."}} {
items.title: Anthropic mathematician claims AI-assisted proof of Riemann Hypothesis; Anthropic stock fell 13.04% on first full trading day

items.summary: OpenAI reported that attacks attempting to extract protected reasoning from an earlier request fell to [q1: 0.2 per cent] in GPT-6.2 Astra, compared with [q2: 54 per cent] under the original safeguards of GPT-6 Astra; success rates for extracting current-request reasoning also declined to [q3: 0.9 per cent] from [q4: 22.9 per cent], according to internal adaptive evaluations involving automated red-teaming. The figures are OpenAI's reported results, not independently verified outcomes. These declines follow upgrades combining model-level safeguards, input and output classifiers, API restrictions, and investigations into coordinated extraction campaigns against multiple unauthorised distillation campaigns detected on its platform in 2026.
items.title: OpenAI reports sharp drop in AI reasoning-extraction attack success after GPT-6 Astra upgrade

items.summary: On November 21, 2026, Oracle stated it had secured the funding needed to fulfill its infrastructure contract with OpenAI, describing itself as the first hyperscaler fully funded for the current investment cycle. The company said financing outlined during its Investor Day—including vendor financing—was already in place and that any further private discussions were additional options rather than requirements. It rejected media reports suggesting its ability to meet the agreement depended on more financing talks. Oracle noted construction at its Abilene campus, where Astra-6 was trained, was nearly complete; its next gigawatt-scale Shackelford campus is fully permitted; and handover of NVIDIA Vera Rubin racks in data halls should begin soon. On financial outlook, it continued to expect positive free cash flow in the second half of fiscal year 2028 and targets more than $30 billion in free cash flow in FY2029, from which it expects to self-fund future growth. The company cautioned that these forward-looking statements are subject to risks and uncertainties.
items.title: Oracle confirms OpenAI contract fully funded and targets over $30 billion free cash flow in FY29

items.summary: The Wall Street Journal reported that SEC enforcement staff are scrutinizing potential accounting issues at Nvidia, though the agency could not confirm the investigation's focus; investigations are not evidence of wrongdoing. Nvidia shares fell about [q1: 13%] on Friday per LSEG data after Reuters published details, having already dropped more than [q2: 6%] before publication. The probe coincides with an extramarital affair involving Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, whom US authorities suspect is a Chinese spy; China denies the allegation. Alice Huang led Singapore-based Megaspeed, which US authorities have investigated since [d1: 2024] over possible export-control violations related to alleged shipments of Nvidia AI chips to China. Megaspeed said Alice Huang left in August [d2: 2025] and conducted 'lawful business.' The crisis sent Nvidia shares tumbling more than a third, though the SEC probe is separate from this decline. Separately, last year Nvidia changed how it reports geographic revenue—using customer headquarters rather than billing addresses—which removed Singapore from its breakdown even as Singapore sales soared to almost half of global revenue; critics link Southeast Asia's role in chip smuggling and circular AI financing deals that complicate investors' assessment of revenue quality and financial exposure. SEC enforcement chief David Woodcock said the agency was examining AI companies' corporate disclosures for full risk disclosure, while interim CEO Colette Kress pledged greater selectivity about future AI industry financing deals.
items.title: SEC probe into Nvidia's accounting draws scrutiny amid Alice Huang scandal and Singapore revenue shift

items.summary: Indian retail investors showed considerable appetite for Anthropic shares after its $81.3 billion initial public offering at a $1.5 trillion valuation, which the report frames as the world's largest public issue so far (per Business Standard). Trading data from INDmoney and Vested placed Anthropic among the most actively traded US equities on Indian platforms; it accounted for 40% of INDmoney's trading activity with average transaction values nearly double the platform average. On Vested, Anthropic contributed approximately 11% of total traded value and 9% of all transactions during the session. A company spokesperson was cited as saying that nearly 84% of trades involving the stock occurred within the opening two hours. The listing attracted professionals from engineering, finance and media, including existing users of Claude AI products, with an average purchase order standing at approximately $1,100 while nearly 20% of active traders bought Anthropic shares. On Vested, Anthropic ranked second by traded value behind AMD but ahead of Nvidia, recording seven times Nvidia's trading activity; however, these cross-platform comparisons mix INDmoney and Vested data on different bases. A US-based investor of Indian origin applied for shares worth more than $130,000 but received an allocation of less than 5% of the requested amount, yet remained optimistic about long-term prospects citing Claude's ability to automate tasks and improve productivity. The listing offered many Indian investors their first opportunity to invest directly in a leading AI model developer; Anthropic shares closed at $97.17 on Thursday, approximately 17.1% above their issue price of $83.
items.title: Anthropic's Indian IPO debut drew strong retail interest amid record-breaking global offering

items.summary: On Friday morning, the S&P 500 was mostly unchanged but on track for a weekly loss of [q3: 5%], its sixth straight day of losses—the longest such streak since COVID-19 began in [d1: 2020]. The Dow rose [q5: 457 points] or [q6: 1%], as it is less exposed to big tech, while the Nasdaq fell [q7: 0.6%]. Anthropic's debut stock fell [q8: 7%] to [q9: $90.55], still above its IPO price of [q10: $83]; the offering at one point surpassed [q11: $2 trillion] in value.
items.title: US Stocks Waver as Tech Sell-off Continues and Anthropic Falls

items.summary: Levent Alpoge, a mathematician at Anthropic, posted on his personal website that he believes he has discovered a proof of the Riemann hypothesis through collaboration with Claude. In his statement, Alpoge said, "I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis," and added that the method extends to the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis and, eventually, the Extended Riemann Hypothesis. He described being left in awe by Claude's ability near the finish line while he guided the work toward an analogous toy setting. The claim remains unverified; Alpoge noted it will be checked by experts before confirming that AI can breach any mathematical frontier. If confirmed, the proof would concern a problem first proposed in 1859 by Bernhard Riemann and one of the few open problems carrying a $1-million bounty from the Clay Mathematics Institute.
items.title: Anthropic Mathematician Claims AI Collaboration Produced a Proof of the Riemann Hypothesis

items.summary: Siddhartha Khemka of Motilal Oswal views the Indian textile sector as constructive, with spinning companies recording a significant earnings recovery—revenue up around 42% YoY and EBITDA rising approximately 98% in 2QFY26, lifting EBITDA margins to about 16% from 11%, supported by high capacity utilization of 98–100% and cotton yarn realizations climbing 21% YoY. Apparel players are benefiting from better order visibility; Gokaldas Exports reported 2QFY27 consolidated revenue growth of 13% to INR11.1b, with EBITDA margins improving 290bp to 9.4%, while Pearl Global saw 2QFY27 revenue grow 37.2% YoY and adjusted EBITDA rise 51.1%. The outlook is supported by improving trade arrangements—US tariff revisions, the extension of AGOA, and agreements with the UK and EU—but realization growth may moderate as volume gains improve; key monitorables include cotton prices, freight and fuel costs, order inflows from the US and Europe, capacity utilization pace, higher cotton costs, and input inflation pass-through. Khemka maintains target prices of 1000 for Gokaldas Exports and 1600 for Pearl Global.
items.title: Siddhartha Khemka sees growth opportunities in Gokaldas Exports and Pearl Global amid textile sector recovery

items.summary: Congress leader Pawan Khera questioned the BJP-led Bihar government for renaming the Kachchi Dargah-Bidupur six-lane bridge after JD(U) leader Nitish Kumar instead of tenth Sikh Guru Guru Gobind Singh, alleging the move tramples Sikh sentiments and suggesting Kumar is being pushed out of the political mainstream. Khera shared an official document showing a non-official resolution moved by RJD leader Tejashwi Yadav on the renaming. Separately, Tejashwi accused the BJP-led Centre of claiming credit for the bridge project despite no contribution to its construction, challenging Prime Minister Narendra Modi's scheduled dedication visit and asserting that Nitish Kumar inaugurated the bridge 17 months ago (described as '1 year and 5 months' in one statement) with hundreds of thousands of vehicles having crossed it. The Nitish Setu is an extradosed cable-stayed bridge over the Ganga, built at a cost of around Rs [q1: 4,280 crore], spanning [q2: 19.7] km to connect Kachchi Dargah on NH-22 in Patna district with Bidupur on NH-322 in Vaishali district, comprising a [q3: 9.7]-km main bridge and [q4: 10 km] of approach roads.
items.title: Congress and RJD contest BJP-led Bihar government's naming of Nitish Setu bridge

items.summary: At IIT Kharagpur's Platinum Jubilee celebrations in West Bengal, Prime Minister Narendra Modi said he cannot let a challenge go unchallenged, framing the statement as an illustration of his approach to overcoming difficulties. Recalling the institution's history, he noted that it stands on a site that once served as a detention camp for freedom fighters and added that their legacy continues to inspire generations of students; he described these camps as having witnessed the courage and determination of Indians who fought for self-rule and envisioned India reaching great heights.
items.title: Modi addresses IIT Kharagpur's 75th anniversary, citing his stance on unchallenged difficulties

items.summary: Barclays recommends investors continue to overweight AI into 2027, though the bank flags emerging dissonances: higher debt funding costs and compute capacity constraints are beginning to pressure project economics and supply chain expectations. The report states that 2027 is when AI starts visibly impacting adopters' income statements, but gains remain marginal in most cases; it fears demand for compute may outrun delivery capacity, forcing investors to reconsider when the technology reaches scale. On macroeconomic grounds, Barclays notes ten-year government bond yields for the US, UK, and Japan are at their highest levels in two decades, pushing borrowing costs to multi-decade highs, with energy prices largely driving central bank actions alongside heavy government borrowing; unresolved excessive debt and hot inflation keep the bank cautious on government bonds and expecting further turbulence. The bank favours US equities—technology, energy, and healthcare sectors—and a blend of momentum, quality, and low-volatility exposure, noting positioning shifts through the year rather than following a static playbook. It also advises revisiting real-asset exposure, particularly infrastructure, to manage supply-driven shocks and growth scares, while pointing to growing opportunities for hedge funds. Barclays concludes that 2027 offers ample opportunity for attractive returns but warns capturing them requires both agility and composure.
items.title: Barclays sees AI as top investment theme in 2027 amid macro headwinds

items.summary: The Immigration Department of Malaysia (JIM) announced via a November 17 notice that visa-free entry for Indian passport holders will end on December 31, 2026, making it mandatory to obtain an approved visa before entering the country from January 1, 2027. Applications may be submitted through MyVISA starting December 1, 2026. The department has not publicly confirmed a specific reason for ending the exemption; reported factors include Malaysia's own introduction of the arrangement and broader tightening of foreign-visa rules since September 2026. India had introduced its 30-day visa-free facility on December 1, 2023 to boost post-COVID tourism, later extending it until December 31, 2026 without announcing a further extension; the exemption was granted for tourism and social visits only. Two months before the notice, in September, India's High Commission in Kuala Lumpur issued an advisory warning nationals against using the tourist visa to seek employment or extend their stay, citing a rise in Indians arriving under the facility seeking work and being misled by agents into overstaying.
items.title: Malaysia to require visas for Indian travellers from January 1, 2027; reasons remain unconfirmed

items.summary: According to a report by The Hindu, motorists in Karnataka can receive a 50% concession [q1] on pending traffic e-challans and Transport Department penalties during a 21-day window running from November 21 to December 11. Additional Superintendent of Police C Mallik stated that all such fines issued between 1991 [d1] and 2025 [d2] are eligible for the discount, covering offences including driving without a seat belt, triple riding, and signal jumping. The initiative aims to clear Mysuru's backlog of traffic and transport fines, with vehicle owners able to check pending cases via the Vahan app.
items.title: Karnataka offers 50% discount on pending e-challans and RTO penalties from November to December

items.summary: The Canada-India Colombo Plan Atomic Reactor Project, signed in April [d1: 1956], was slated to cost [q1: 14.5 million Canadian] dollars but ultimately increased by [q10: 5 million Canadian] dollars and fell more than two years behind schedule after construction began. The reactor, named CIRUS (Canada-India Reactor Utility Services) and modelled on Canada's Chalk River facility, was built in Trombay near Bombay to help India acquire expertise for its own reactors. More than [q3: 700 construction] workers were employed at the site; one reporter described their wages of just one rupee and [q4: 50 paise] a day as equivalent in purchasing power to about [q5: 170 rupees] today, conditions Canadian engineers said they had no business interfering with. Eventually, [q7: 30 Canadian] scientists worked on the project over more than four years. The reactor first went critical in July [d6: 1960], was inaugurated by Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru six months later, and its inauguration took place in January [d7: 1961]. Canada suspended nuclear cooperation with India after New Delhi conducted its first nuclear test using plutonium from the CIRUS reactor's spent fuel in [d8: 1974], halting bilateral engagement for three decades. The partnership was revived following a US civil nuclear agreement signed in [d9: 2008]. In [d10: 2026], New Delhi and Ottawa signed a C$[q11: 2.6 billion uranium] supply agreement under which Cameco Corp will supply [q12: 10,000 tonnes] of uranium concentrate over nine years beginning in [d11: 2027]. The CIRUS reactor was finally shut down in December [d12: 2010].
